newsitem.title: USA: White House official meets anti-tobacco negotiator.
newsitem.headline: White House official meets anti-tobacco negotiator.

text.p: A senior White House official met Tuesday with Mississippi Attorney General Michael Moore, a key negotiator in settlement talks between anti-smoking forces and tobacco companies.
White House deputy counsel Bruce Lindsey received an update on the settlement talks from Moore, said a White House official who asked to remain unidentified.
Talks between top industry executives, states and a scattering of anti-tobacco forces began about two weeks ago concerning a settlement of suits by 22 states.
The parties are probably going to meet again later this week, the White House official said.

The industry has been considering paying as much as a reported $300 billion over 25 years into a compensation fund for smokers who fall sick with lung cancer and other diseases. In return, the industry would get broad shelter from lawsuits.
President Bill Clinton on Sunday left open the possibility he could endorse a deal protecting tobacco companies from being sued by smokers whose health has been damaged.
"I think we ought to see what kind of agreement they come up with and let me submit it to the public health experts and see what they say," Clinton said in an interview on CBS's "Face the Nation."
Clinton is closely monitoring the settlement talks to ensure that politically risky steps he took to increase federal oversight of the industry are protected.

Last year he gave broad powers to the federal Food and Drug Administration by approving its contention that nicotine is a drug. That position underpins the FDA's effort to regulate the industry and limit advertising it considers to be aimed at persuading young people to smoke.
The tobacco industry is fighting that regulatory effort in court, but there have been reports that the industry negotiators were considering dropping their challenge.
Last Friday, a federal judge in Greensboro, N.C., ruled the FDA can regulate sales and labeling of cigarettes, but that it had no authority over advertising.
